Fundamentalism is the strong, unwavering belief that a particular set of core principles — usually from a religion or ideology — must be followed exactly as they were originally stated, without any change, reinterpretation, or compromise, regardless of how the world changes around them.

Think of it this way: imagine a rulebook written hundreds of years ago. A fundamentalist believes that rulebook must be followed word for word, forever, and that any attempt to update, adapt, or reread it in a modern context is wrong, dangerous, or even sinful.
The word "fundamentalism" can apply to religion, politics, and even certain ideologies. However, it is most commonly used in the context of religion.

This is where the term is used the most. Religious fundamentalism means a strict, literal belief in the sacred texts of a religion — like the Bible, the Quran, or the Torah — and a rejection of any modern interpretation that softens, questions, or changes those texts.

A religious fundamentalist believes:

  • Their holy scripture is 100% literally true.
  • The original rules and laws laid down in that text must govern life today, just as they did centuries ago.
  • Modernism, secularism, and liberal thinking are threats to their faith.
  • There is no room for doubt, debate, or flexible interpretation.

For example, a Christian fundamentalist might insist that the Earth was created in exactly six days, exactly as described in the Bible — not as a metaphor, not as a poetic story, but as a literal fact. A Islamic fundamentalist might insist that all laws of society must come directly and strictly from the Quran and early Islamic legal tradition, with no influence from modern democratic or secular thinking.

It is important to note that fundamentalism exists across virtually all major world religions — Christianity, Islam, Judaism, Hinduism, Sikhism, and others all have fundamentalist movements within them.

No matter which religion or ideology it appears in, fundamentalism tends to share certain defining features:

1. Literalism. The text means exactly what it says. No metaphor, no context, no reinterpretation. If the text says the Earth is flat, a fundamentalist believes the Earth is flat.

2. Absolutism. There is only one truth — theirs. Other views are not just different; they are wrong, corrupt, or evil.

3. Resistance to change. The modern world, with its evolving values and new scientific discoveries, is seen as a corrupting force. The fundamentalist wants to hold the line firmly against it.

4. A sense of threat. Fundamentalism often intensifies when a group feels that its beliefs, culture, or identity are under attack. It is frequently a reaction — a pushback against liberalism, modernity, or outside influence.

5. Clear in-group vs. out-group thinking. "We are the true believers. Everyone else has gone astray." This sharp division between "us" (the pure, faithful) and "them" (the corrupt, the lost) is a hallmark of fundamentalist thinking.

6. Authority of the original source. Whether it is a holy book, a founding document, or an ancient tradition, fundamentalists treat their original source of truth as the highest possible authority — above science, above courts, above modern governments.

This is crucial to understand: fundamentalism does not automatically mean violence or terrorism. This is one of the biggest misconceptions about the word.

Many fundamentalists are peaceful, law-abiding people who simply live by very strict religious rules, keep to their own communities, avoid outside influences, and raise their families according to their beliefs. They might refuse to watch television, send their children to secular schools, or socialise with outsiders — but they do not harm anyone.

On the other end of the spectrum, some fundamentalist movements do become extreme and dangerous. When fundamentalist beliefs combine with political power and a willingness to use force, they can lead to violence, terrorism, or oppressive regimes. But this is the extreme end — not the definition of fundamentalism itself.

Think of fundamentalism as a sliding scale:

Strict but peaceful private observance → Social separatism → Political activism → Militant extremism

The word "fundamentalism" covers a wide portion of that scale, but it does not automatically land at the violent end.
How Fundamentalism Differs from Similar Words

Since you want to understand this fully, it helps to compare it to nearby ideas so you can see exactly where fundamentalism sits:

Orthodoxy means strictly following the traditional, accepted beliefs of a religion. It is about staying true to established doctrine. Orthodoxy is normal and widely accepted within many religions. Fundamentalism goes further — it is more rigid, more defensive, more reactive, and more likely to view the outside world as an enemy.

Conservatism (in a religious sense) means preferring traditional practices over new ones. A conservative believer might resist change but is often open to some adjustment over time. A fundamentalist typically rejects any adjustment at all.

Radicalism means pushing for extreme or revolutionary change — it can be in any direction. Fundamentalism is usually anti-change, so while some fundamentalists can become radical (especially politically), the words are not synonyms.

Extremism refers to holding views that are far outside the mainstream, often combined with a willingness to take extreme actions. Not all fundamentalists are extremists. But when fundamentalism crosses into violence or hatred, it enters the territory of extremism.

The word has also been stretched to apply outside religion when someone follows a non-religious ideology with the same rigid, uncompromising, all-or-nothing intensity.

For instance:

  • Market fundamentalism refers to the absolute belief that free markets must never be regulated or interfered with — that the market is always right, no exceptions. (This is also called laissez-faire thinking taken to its extreme.)
  • Political fundamentalism refers to rigidly following a political ideology as if it were sacred scripture, refusing to compromise, question, or update it.

In these non-religious uses, the word carries the same core meaning: uncompromising, rigid adherence to a set of core beliefs as though they are absolute and beyond question.

Understanding why it happens helps you understand it more deeply.

Fundamentalism typically emerges when a community feels:

  • Threatened — by modernisation, secularism, foreign cultures, or political change.
  • Lost — when rapid social change leaves people without a clear sense of identity or moral order.
  • Disrespected — when a group feels its beliefs are being mocked, marginalised, or eroded.

In this sense, fundamentalism is often a defensive reaction — a way of drawing a firm line in the sand and saying, "This is who we are. This is what we believe. And we will not let it be taken from us."

If you had to explain "fundamentalism" in three sentences to someone:

Fundamentalism is the belief that the original, core rules of a religion or ideology must be followed exactly and without change, no matter what the modern world says. Fundamentalists treat their founding texts or principles as absolute, perfect truth — not open to reinterpretation. It is a rigid, uncompromising way of thinking that often arises when people feel their beliefs or identity are under threat.
